# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-15 (Extended v124)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826. **Current narrative point (Autumn Year 4, evening—crisis at Gorbeau house escalating, immediate aftermath)**: Paris—Gorbeau house (50-52, Salpêtrière district); Luxembourg gardens; le Petit-Picpus convent; M. Gillenormand's residences; English provincial towns (Dunstead, Staveford, Kelmere, Torton, Ostcombe, Ravenmere, Kelford, Yarlby, Gulhaven, Wilwick, Wilholt, Quenford). **Current environmental**: Smoke from chimneys lies flat over fields; frost silvered hedges overnight; bell for vespers rings thinly across roofs; light went early; icy breeze; wind off water carries salt/tar scent; gulls quarrel over fish heads; rain threatened since morning, holds off; road all ruts and puddles after thaw; someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall; cart loaded with turnips creaked past well; bees hum in lavender behind parsonage; dog barks at nothing then goes quiet.

## Primary Locations
**GORBEAU HOUSE**: 50-52 Salpêtrière district. **JONDRETTE DEN**: Abject, fetid, sordid. Furniture: straw chair, infirm table, crockery, two pallets, straw beds. Walls: leprous, seamed, obscene charcoal sketches, repulsive moisture. Fireplace with brazier filled burning charcoal (glowing hot, red with blue flame), pot, broken boards, suspended rags, bird-cage. Dormer window (four broken panes). Colored engraving "THE DREAM" (sleeping woman/child, eagle, Napoleon on blue column). **Wooden panel—Battle of Waterloo painting: sergeant rescuer (Thénardier) carrying colonel victim (Pontmercy) amid smoke.** Two heaps: old iron/ropes and rope-ladder with wooden rungs and two hooks. Verdigris candlestick with burning candle.

## Crisis at Gorbeau House: Sequence and Resolution
**M. Leblanc's initial struggle**: Overturned chair and table, moved toward window with prodigious agility. Six robust fists seized him—three "chimney-builders" dragged him back. Thénardier woman wound hands in his hair. Herculean struggle: M. Leblanc knocked old man tumbling, overthrew two more with backward hand sweeps. Four others seized him by both arms and back of neck.

**M. Leblanc bound with ropes**: Despite binding, surrounded, half plunged in grave, M. Leblanc remained impassive—soul inaccessible to terror. Preserved silence, carried precaution of forgetting anxiety for own life. **Marius found this superbly melancholy visage and extraordinary composure deeply troubling.**

**Thénardier's metamorphosis**: Transformed from ferocious robber into polished negotiator—moderated language, subdued, crafty, reserved, choice diction. Marius difficult recognizing tiger converted into lawyer. **Thénardier's scheme**: Wife will dress as before and hunt up "the Lark" (Cosette) with letter from M. Leblanc. Girl will follow into carriage. Outside barrier, trap with two horses waits. Young lady will alight from fiacre; Thénardier's comrade will enter other vehicle with her; wife returns to report completion. **Threat**: "If you have me arrested, my comrade will give a turn of his thumb to the Lark, that's all." **Deliberate name avoidance**: Thénardier avoided naming girl—precaution of clever man.

**M. Leblanc's address demanded**: Thénardier instructed M. Leblanc to write letter addressed "Mademoiselle Fabre" to his house. "I know that you live a long distance from here, near Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas, because you go to mass there every day, but I don't know in what street."

**M. Leblanc's extraordinary act (turning point)**: Before seven men could collect senses, M. Leblanc bent down into fireplace, stretched out hand to brazier, straightened himself up. **Brandished above his head the red-hot chisel, emitting threatening glow**—almost free and in formidable attitude. Thénardier, female Thénardier, and ruffians huddled in amazement at extremity of hovel, stared in stupefaction.

**Means of escape**: Prisoner had coin piece on person when searched; contrived to conceal it in hand; having right hand free, unscrewed it and used as saw to cut cords—explaining faint noise Marius had observed.

**Marius's response**: Reeled in utter horror. Very ruffians shuddered. Hardly muscle of old man's face contracted. While red-hot iron sank into smoking wound, **impassive and almost august, he fixed on Thénardier his beautiful glance, in which there was no hatred, and where suffering vanished in serene majesty.**

**Javert's ambush and M. Leblanc's final escape**: Javert (tall man, square face, thin firm mouth, thick gray ferocious whiskers) positioned outside Gorbeau house with men. At nightfall, posted young girls as lookouts; "caged" Azelma—Éponine disappeared, not at post. Grew impatient, decided to go upstairs without waiting for Marius's pistol-shot signal. **Took action before Marius fired.** Ruffians terrified, flung themselves on arms abandoned in corners—one with meat-axe, another with key, another with bludgeon, rest with shears, pincers, hammers. Thénardier had knife in fist. **Thénardier woman snatched enormous paving-stone from angle of window (daughters' ottoman), hurled at Javert's head. Javert ducked; stone passed over him, struck wall behind, knocked off huge piece of plastering.** **M. Leblanc's escape during chaos**: Door was guarded, but window was not. As soon as released from bonds and while Javert drawing up report, took advantage of confusion, crowd, darkness, moment when general attention diverted from him, to dash out of window.

## Marius Pontmercy: Crisis of Conscience (Unresolved)
**Identity and age**: Baron Marius Pontmercy, twenty years old; three years estranged from grandfather. **Paternal legacy**: Colonel's written instruction regarding baron title and Waterloo sergeant Thénardier. Lost medallion of black shagreen. **Now recognized**: Thénardier depicted in Waterloo painting—sergeant who rescued father at Waterloo.

**Unprecedented perplexity (evening crisis)**: For last hour had two voices in conscience—one enjoining him to respect father's testament, other crying to rescue prisoner. Two voices continued uninterrupted struggle tormenting him to agony. Up to that moment cherished vague hope of reconciling two duties, but nothing within limits of possibility presented itself. **Had not time for deliberation—scene hastening to catastrophe. He was on verge of swooning. Knees gave way beneath him. Last possibility of doubt vanished. Certainly was Thénardier of the will.**

**Critical moral dilemma**: Everything depended on Marius. Unknown to themselves, he held all beings in his hand. If he fired pistol, M. Leblanc saved, Thénardier lost; if he did not fire, M. Leblanc sacrificed. Remorse awaited him either case. Father once saved by Thénardier at Waterloo—sergeant rescued colonel. Yet M. Leblanc now victim of Thénardier's ambush. Moral obligation to both: honor father's will AND prevent crime against innocent man and Cosette's father. **Crisis of conscience at absolute peak; outcome unclear.**

## Girl (Cosette) and M. Leblanc Identity
**Girl identity clarified**: Handkerchief bore letters U. F., which meant Urbain Fabre, not Ursule. M. Leblanc is Monsieur Fabre—the girl's biological father. Cosette became convent scholar; believes Valjean is her father; adores him. **Marius now recognizes**: The "girl" he worshipped for six months is Cosette, whom he encountered again miraculously in hovel as charitable visitor with M. Leblanc. She is also being held captive by Thénardier's scheme.

## Jean Valjean
Valjean integrated as convent assistant gardener; inhabits old garden hut with Fauchelevent. Spiritual transformation complete. Fauchelevent sole ally aware of full presence.

## English Provincial Towns: Mundane Activities
**Town movements**: Peten Haskick broke faith with Luwyn Brackick; promised work (pay old debt owed to Prydenridge family) never begun. **Peten Haskick found work in Quenford, moved there, and did not return to Staveford.** **Lura Haskick followed him to Quenford within the month.** **Kadrek went along to live in Wilholt. Only daughter of Zalis Corrley left Torton and settled in Wilholt.** Stenworth and Prydenridge families: Pelde Stenson, Davus Stenworth, Fewyn Stenworth, Havus Stenworth, Dalis, Yera Stenworth, Nerine Prydenridge, Luvie Prydenridge, Zavus Prydenridge, Vesmira Thornmere, Wenelle Lindmere (gave up idleness, took work as chandler), Isric Thornmere. **Fewyn Stenworth argued with carter over price of sack of oats.** Daily activities: sorting old letters, mending torn sleeves, scrubbing steps, humming childhood tunes. Conversations: weather, harvest, lame horse, rain, river up, price of salt. Baker's boy late again; line at oven grew long. Children chased hoop down lane, shrieking. Almanac read aloud.

## Historical Context: The Restoration and Revolution of July (1815-1832)
**Bourbon Restoration critique**: After Napoleon fell, House of Bourbon returned to France. Believed it bestowed rights and could take back charter rights. Did not suspect roots of French society not fixed in Bourbons but in nations. Bourbons were illustrious and bleeding knot in history, but no longer principal element of destiny, necessary base of politics. France could get along without them; had done without them for twenty-two years. Never had princes been so blind in presence of facts and divine authority contained therein.

**Restoration's fatal decision (1830)**: When Restoration supposing itself victorious and well-rooted, abruptly decided on its plan of action and risked its stroke. One morning it drew itself up before France, elevated its voice, contested collective title and individual right of nation to sovereignty, of citizen to liberty. Denied to nation that which made it a nation, denied to citizen that which made him citizen.

**Fifteen years of intellectual progress (1815-1830)**: Under Restoration, nation had grown accustomed to calm discussion lacking under Republic, to grandeur in peace lacking under Empire. France free and strong offered encouraging spectacle to other peoples of Europe. Revolution had word under Robespierre; cannon had word under Bonaparte; under Louis XVIII and Charles X, intelligence had word. For fifteen years, great principles—so old for thinker, so new for statesman—could be seen at work in perfect peace: equality before law, liberty of conscience, speech, press, accessibility of all aptitudes to all functions. Thus it proceeded until 1830. **The Bourbons were instrument of civilization which broke in hands of Providence.**

**Revolution of July (1830): Reception and character**: Instantly had friends and enemies throughout entire world. First rushed toward her with joy and enthusiasm; others turned away. Princes of Europe, owls of this dawn, shut eyes, wounded and stupefied, only opened them to threaten. **Fright comprehensible, wrath pardoned.** Strange revolution had hardly produced shock; had not even paid vanquished royalty honor of treating it as enemy, shedding blood. In eyes of despotic governments (always interested in having liberty calumniate itself), Revolution of July committed fault of being formidable and remaining gentle. Nothing attempted or plotted against it. Most discontented, most irritated, most trembling, saluted it; mysterious respect springs from events in which we sense collaboration of someone working above man.

**Philosophical reflection on Right vs. Fact**: Property of right is to remain eternally beautiful and pure. Fact, even when most necessary, most thoroughly accepted by contemporaries, if exist only as fact, if contain only too little of right or none, infallibly destined in course of time to become deformed, impure, perhaps monstrous. Machiavelli example: not evil genius nor demon nor miserable writer—nothing but fact. Not only Italian fact; European fact of sixteenth century. Seems hideous in presence of moral idea of nineteenth.

**"Statesmen" and political mediocrity**: Skilful in our century conferred on themselves title of Statesmen. Word has become somewhat of slang. Wherever nothing but skill, necessarily pettiness. "The skilful" amounts to "the mediocre." To say "statesmen" sometimes equivalent to saying "traitors." According to skilful, revolutions like Revolution of July are severed arteries; prompt ligature indispensable. Right too grandly proclaimed shaken. Right once firmly fixed, state must be strengthened. Liberty once assured, attention directed to power.

**Post-revolution necessity of dynasty**: Politicians ingenious in putting mask of necessity on profitable fictions claim first requirement of people after revolution, when part of monarchical continent, is to procure dynasty. Thus say they, peace—time to dress wounds, repair house—can be had after revolution. Dynasty conceals scaffolding, covers ambulance. Not always easy to procure dynasty. King resulting from revolution may be and useful to be revolutionary—participant in own person in that revolution, lent hand to it, compromised or distinguished himself therein, touched axe or wielded sword in it.

**Art of retarding progress**: Great art lies in making little render to success sound of catastrophe, so those profiting tremble from it also; seasoning with fear every step taken; augmenting curve of transition to point of retarding progress; dulling that aurora; denouncing and retrenching harshness of enthusiasm; cutting all angles and nails; wadding triumph; muffling up right; enveloping giant-people in flannel; putting it to bed speedily; imposing diet on excess of health; putting Hercules on treatment of convalescent; diluting event with expedient; offering to spirits thirsting for ideal that nectar thinned out with potion; taking precautions against too much success; garnishing revolution with shade.

**Bourgeois aspiration after 1830**: State to which part of nation called bourgeoisie aspired after shock of 1830 was not inertia complicated with indifference and laziness containing little shame, nor slumber presupposing momentary forgetfulness accessible to dreams—was the halt.
